In comparison to other methods commonly used for multi-species bacterial comparative genomics, bofasa is substantially more conservative in predicting orthology yet can often recover the largest single-copy core genome. Beyond orthology inference, the software also features several additional utility functionalities, including assessment of which ortholog groups are commonly found on mobile genetic elements or possess variable genomic contexts.

papers.title: Phage peptide promotes bacterial cell death via inner and outer membrane targets
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) play a major role in mammalian innate immunity by preferentially targeting bacterial membranes through charge-dependent interactions. While CAMPs are extensively studied in eukaryotic systems, less is known about phage-encoded CAMPs and their role in bacterial lysis. Here, we characterize gp28, a 56-aa cationic peptide encoded by the T7-like coliphage phiKT to define its mechanism of membrane disruption and bacteriostatic activity. Biochemical fractionation reveals that gp28 is asymmetrically distributed across bacterial membranes. Supporting its direct role in causing cell death, gp28 induces permeability changes at the inner membrane. Using synthetic gp28 peptide, we also show that gp28 activity is blocked by lipopolysaccharide and divalent cation competition. This led us to discover that gp28 is also active against Gram-positive bacteria in a surface charge-dependent manner. Finally, we demonstrate gp28 has broad bacteriostatic activity against multiple Gram-negative species, including clinical Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) isolates. Together, our results support a model in which gp28 exploits charge-based interactions with bacterial surface molecules to gain access to membranes, then destabilizes the envelope to promote host cell death. These findings expand our understanding of phage lysis strategies and highlight phage-derived peptides as potential scaffolds for antimicrobial development. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Cationic antimicrobial peptides produced by eukaryotes target and disrupt bacterial membranes. These peptides are integral members of the innate immune system and potential antibacterials. Due to their cellular origin, the genetics to understand their mechanisms of action are cumbersome. Here, we demonstrate functional similarity between a bacteriophage peptide called gp28 and cationic antimicrobial peptides. Gp28 partitions between both membranes of Gram-negative bacteria and reduces their integrity. We show that gp28 employs charge-based interactions to associate with and disrupt membranes, suggesting that gp28 targets charged polymers on the membrane surface. Additionally, gp28 inhibits the growth of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, and renders them more susceptible to antibiotics. Our studies provide a foundation for future genetics and development of phage peptide-based antimicrobials.

papers.title: Single-cell Profiling of Airway-associated CD4+ T cells in Metal-induced Hypersensitivity
papers.abstract: Omics-based approaches are increasingly used to identify unique molecular signatures that may serve as biomarkers for early disease detection and potential therapeutic targets. Chronic beryllium disease (CBD), resulting from beryllium-induced hypersensitivity, is characterized by the accumulation and expansion of pathogenic CD4+ T cells in the lungs, ultimately contributing to impaired pulmonary function. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on sorted viable bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cells from beryllium-exposed patients (n=2) and compared their transcriptional profiles with publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from healthy controls (n=10). We identified 11 distinct CD3-associated cell clusters comprising T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and regulatory T cells. Further analysis of CD4+ T cells from beryllium-exposed patients revealed increased expression of genes associated with T cell activation, immune regulation, and persistence, including IFNG, TNF, TNFAIP3, and CD74. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis further revealed upregulation of pathways associated with cellular activation, immune responses, and immune effector functions, whereas pathways related to metabolic processes were downregulated in beryllium samples compared with healthy controls. Overall, our findings identify distinct transcriptional signatures, including IFI27 and FABP4, in CD4+ T cells from beryllium-exposed patients, providing insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying beryllium-induced pulmonary inflammation and highlighting potential candidates for further investigation as disease biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

papers.title: COVID-19 and Active Tuberculosis Exhibit Distinct Maturation-Associated Neutrophil Transcriptional Programs
papers.abstract: Neutrophils can promote pathogen control or drive tissue-damaging inflammation, but the mechanisms that determine these divergent outcomes remain poorly defined. COVID-19 and active tuberculosis (TB) offer a purposeful comparison since both are pulmonary infections with substantial neutrophil involvement, yet differ in pathogen class, inflammatory duration, and the balance between neutrophil-associated host defense and pathology. We therefore tested whether their divergent neutrophil programs align with distinct maturation-associated transcriptional states. We integrated six publicly available whole-blood bulk RNA-sequencing datasets, comprising three COVID-19 and three active TB cohorts. A curated panel of 770 genes covered activation, degranulation, neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation, chemotaxis, cell surface receptors, and maturation. Study-associated variation was reduced using ComBat-Seq, and differential expression relative to disease-appropriate controls was assessed with DESeq2. Most genes changed in the same direction in both diseases, but 348 (45.2%) differed significantly in response magnitude, with 159 genes showing a stronger response in COVID-19 and 189 in TB. COVID-19 samples showed reduced expression of the maturation markers CD10 (MME) and CD16 (FCGR3A), alongside elevated expression of granule-cargo and NET-associated genes, including MPO and ELANE, consistent with a greater contribution from immature, emergency granulopoiesis-derived neutrophil populations. In contrast, TB samples showed higher maturation-associated, receptor, oxidative, and recruitment responses, consistent with a relatively mature receptor-competent neutrophil transcriptional signature. Independent COVID-19 Ward and pulmonary TB cohorts showed directional agreement for maturation and NET-associated signatures (100% and 90% concordance, respectively), while chemotaxis and select receptor and degranulation genes showed weaker reproducibility indicating that maturation represents the most consistently reproduced axis of distinction between the two diseases. Together, these findings identify maturation-associated transcription as the most consistently reproduced axis distinguishing COVID-19 from TB. These signatures provide candidate biomarkers for future studies linking neutrophil states to clinical outcomes and informing host-directed therapeutic strategies that preserve antimicrobial function while limiting immunopathology.

papers.title: Fast, accurate construction of multiple sequence alignments from protein language embeddings
papers.abstract: Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) is a foundational task in computational biology, underpinning protein structure prediction, evolutionary analysis, and domain annotation. Traditional MSA algorithms rely on pairwise amino acid substitution matrices derived from conserved protein families. While effective for aligning closely related sequences, these scoring schemes struggle in the low-identity ``twilight zone.'' Here, we present a new approach for constructing MSAs leveraging amino acid embeddings generated by protein language models (PLMs), which capture rich evolutionary and contextual information from massive and diverse sequence datasets. We introduce a windowed reciprocal-weighted embedding similarity metric that is surprisingly effective in identifying corresponding amino acids across sequences. Building on this metric, we develop ARIES (Alignment via RecIprocal Embedding Similarity), an algorithm that constructs a PLM-generated template embedding and aligns each sequence to this template via dynamic time warping in order to build a global MSA. Across diverse benchmark datasets, ARIES achieves higher accuracies than existing state-of-the-art approaches, especially in low-identity regimes where traditional methods degrade, while scaling almost linearly with the number of sequences to be aligned. Together, these results provide the first large-scale demonstration of the power of PLMs for accurate and scalable MSA construction across protein families of varying sizes and levels of similarity, highlighting the potential of PLMs to transform comparative sequence analysis.

papers.title: Neuronal Hyperexcitability and Seizure Susceptibility in a Novel Kcnt1 G269S Mouse Model
papers.abstract: KCNT1-related epilepsy is an autosomal dominant neurodevelopmental disorder resulting from de novo pathogenic variants in KCNT1 which encodes a sodium-gated potassium channel. To date, 64 KCNT1 mutations have been identified across 248 individuals. The majority of pathogenic KCNT1 mutations are gain-of-function (GOF), with each exhibiting unique channel biophysical properties, channel dynamics, electrophysiological spiking, and epileptiform characteristics. These diverse neuronal electrical profiles, contribute to a spectrum of epilepsy syndromes ranging from severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathies to focal epilepsies with milder outcomes. Among these, variants at Gly288 are recurrent, reported in 29 of 248 individuals in the largest published cohort to date, and 79% (23/29) of whom presented with severe early-onset epilepsy, yet no in vivo model of this pore-domain variant currently exists. Our multi-disciplinary collaboration generated a novel mouse model (C57BL/6-Kcnt1em1Bryd) that carries the G269S variant of Kcnt1, corresponding to the human G288S variant, located within the coding region of the channel pore. We characterized network excitability of primary cultured cortical neurons from all three genotypes (Kcnt1+/+, Kcnt1+/G269S, and Kcnt1G269S/G269S) on high-density microelectrode arrays, since many KCNT1 mouse models require homozygosity for phenotypic detection. Kcnt1+/G269S neurons exhibited sustained hyperexcitability and hypersynchronous bursting versus Kcnt1+/+ controls, while Kcnt1G269S/G269S neurons showed early excessive bursting followed by a progressive decline in coordinated network activity by 28 days-in-vitro. Therefore, behavioral comparisons were conducted between Kcnt1+/G269S and Kcnt1+/+ mice including developmental milestones, motor and cognitive abilities, respiratory physiology, and seizure susceptibility. Kcnt1+/G269S mice exhibited spontaneous behavioral seizures, poor motor coordination, erratic breathing, and increased apneas, as functional outcome measures. Critically, Kcnt1+/G269S mice were more susceptible to thermal-induced seizures in early life and chemoconvulsant induced seizures in adulthood. In summary, these data: (i) generated and validated a novel mouse model of KCNT1-related epilepsy, (ii) provide strong in vitro evidence of neuronal hyperexcitability, (iii) illustrate behavioral spontaneous seizures, early-life seizures, and adult seizure susceptibility as functional outcome measures, (iv) elucidated alterations in exploratory locomotion and poor motor coordination, (v) identified increased erratic breathing in female and increased apneas in male Kcnt1+/G269S mice and (vi) lay the groundwork for future analysis of neural activity in vivo and modeling circuit level dynamics in vitro, in vivo, and in silico.

papers.title: CD19 CAR T cell therapy reshapes the host microbiota immune axis in autoimmune diseases
papers.abstract: CD19 targeted CAR T cell therapy induces profound B cell depletion and clinical responses in autoimmune disease; however, whether it reshapes host microbiota interactions remains unknown. We longitudinally profiled gut microbiome composition and microbiota-specific humoral immunity in 20 patients with systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic sclerosis, or idiopathic inflammatory myopathy undergoing CAR T cell therapy, alongside 23 healthy controls, using shotgun metagenomics, IgA/IgG-bound microbiota profiling, and PhIP Seq. CAR T cell therapy reshaped microbiota directed humoral immunity, with reduced fecal IgA and serum anti commensal IgA and IgG accompanied by selective remodeling of microbiota-reactive antibody repertoires. This finding was paralleled by selective changes in gut microbial composition, including depletion of Bifidobacterium adolescentis, without uniform depletion of disease-associated pathobionts. Integrated host microbiome analyses identified altered predicted protein protein interactions involving the immunoproteasome and B cell plasma cell pathways, with interactions before CAR T cell intervention being significantly associated with subsequent relapse. Consistent with these findings, taxon specific IgA targeting, but not global diversity of IgA IgG coated microbiota, differed according to subsequent relapse. Lower baseline fecal IgA was also associated with delayed B-cell reconstitution, linking mucosal humoral immunity to immune recovery after CAR T cell therapy.

papers.title: RNAbridge: a database of extended non-canonical helices
papers.abstract: RNA function is dictated by 3D architecture. Although 2D structural models based on canonical Watson-Crick base pairs are widely used, they often fail to capture the non-canonical interactions, tertiary contacts, and coaxial stacking important for biological activity. We have developed RNAbridge, a comprehensive database and web application that systematically identifies, quantifies, and visualizes extended non-canonical helices and multi-way junctions ("non-canonical" denoting the interruptions between canonical stems rather than non-canonical pairing within them). Using a geometry- and stacking-based pipeline, we analyzed the Protein Data Bank and compiled a catalog of 153,148 structural elements, with a representative view of 7,453 elements. In this view, 4,998 multi-segment extended helices and junction arrangements have measurable bend angles, and 2,455 are single-segment canonical stem-loops. RNAbridge includes a user-friendly interface with interactive filters, synchronized 2D and 3D visualizations, and detailed structural data, including helical bend angles and stacking paths. By connecting simplified 2D topologies with complex 3D structures, RNAbridge serves as a valuable resource for structural biologists and lays the foundation for future machine learning applications in RNA structure prediction. The database, available at https://rnabridge.cs.put.poznan.pl/, is automatically updated once a week. All counts reported here refer to the November 8, 2026 release.

papers.title: Peripheral detection of viruses shapes brain immunity and behavior in zebrafish
papers.abstract: Olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) are constantly exposed to pathogens, including viruses. However, serious brain infection via the olfactory route rarely occurs. When OSNs detect a virus, they coordinate local antiviral immune responses to stop virus progression to the brain. Despite effective immune control in the olfactory periphery, pathogen-triggered neuronal signals reach the CNS via the olfactory bulb (OB). We hypothesized that neuronal detection of a virus by OSNs initiates neuroimmune responses in the OB that prevent pathogen invasion. Using zebrafish (Danio rerio) as a model, we demonstrate viral-specific neuronal activation of OSNs projecting into the OB, indicating that OSNs are electrically activated by viruses. Further, behavioral changes are seen in both adult and larval zebrafish after viral exposure. By profiling the transcription of single cells in the OB after OSNs are exposed to virus, we found that both microglia and neurons enter a protective state. Microglia and macrophage populations in the OB respond within minutes of nasal viral delivery followed decreased expression of neuronal differentiation factors and enrichment of genes in the neuropeptide signaling pathway in neuronal clusters. Pituitary adenylate-cyclase-activating polypeptide (pacap), a known antimicrobial, was especially enriched in a neuronal cluster. We confirm that PACAP is antiviral in vitro and that PACAP expression increases in the OB 1 day post-viral treatment. Our work reveals how encounters with viruses in the olfactory periphery shape the vertebrate brain by inducing antimicrobial programs in neurons and by altering host behavior.

papers.title: Kymograph classifiers predict CMT2A disease-relevant mitochondrial motility phenotypes in iPSC motor neurons
papers.abstract: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A (CMT2A) is a genetic disease characterized by autosomal dominant MFN2 mutations and dysregulated mitochondrial trafficking. While there is currently no FDA-approved CMT2A therapy, the recent development of iPSC motor neuron model systems, high-throughput imaging platforms, and CRISPR-based gene editing technologies holds promise for screening new therapies at scale in vitro. A critical roadblock for therapeutic screening is the development of scalable and robust computational methods to assess the mitochondrial trafficking phenotypes, healthy or diseased, of each iPSC motor neuron sample. To address this gap, we developed a vision transformer (ViT) based classification framework that predicts disease phenotypes using kymographs, an image transformation that captures particle movement along a prespecified path, such as mitochondrial movement along axons. We show that our classification approach more accurately discriminates healthy MFN2 wild-type (WT) from diseased MFN2 R364W-mutant (R364W) iPSCs than alternative summary statistics, such as mitochondrial speed and fraction of stationary mitochondria that are directly extracted from kymographs. Furthermore, we show that our model maintains high accuracy when deployed on a biological replicate holdout dataset. An analysis of ViT patch embeddings of the kymographs shows that mitochondria with highly variable sizes and many intersection events most strongly associate with R364W diseased kymographs. The computational approach demonstrated in this paper has broad applicability for future high-throughput screens where organelle trafficking along axons plays a key role in disease pathogenesis.

papers.title: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop
papers.abstract: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.

papers.title: BenchmarkHub: an open-source platform for reproducible evaluation of large language models in healthcare
papers.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are solely judged by their scores on biomedical benchmarks, yet these scores are rarely reproducible since the prompts, inference settings and model builds are seldom reported. We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source platform for auditable evaluation of language and vision-language models for biomedical research. Methods: BenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub. The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records. The platform samples questions with fixed seeds, runs models directly or as tool-using agents in a code sandbox, grades answers with deterministic rules and stores every prompt, reply and tool call. The interface provides a leaderboard to rank performance of the models, allowing model comparison without any preexisting programming knowledge. Findings: We used BenchmarkHub to evaluate 12 open-weight models in five experiments on 15 biomedical benchmarks (11 text, two multimodal and two computational biology) and two general benchmarks. The pooled accuracy ranged from 46.1% (95% CI 43.0-49.3) to 80.9% (78.3-83.3). Re-grading the responses with simple answer-extraction rules lowered a model's accuracy by up to 33.1 percentage points, leading to a reorder of the leaderboard. Published scores were found for 23 out of the 143 benchmark/model combinations tested. The accuracy measured by BenchmarkHub was lower than in the published results in 19 out of the 23 available comparisons. The effect of four prompting protocols (1: default prompt; 2: asking the model to answer the letter only; 3: chain-of-thought prompting; 4: three-shot prompting) changed MedQA accuracy by up to 11.3 points but was not significant after multiple-testing correction with 150 questions. We also tested the impact of ablation on benchmarking using the MMMU benchmark dataset. Removing images lowered the accuracy by 18.0 and 19.3 points respectively for the two strongest models. Finally, the accuracy of agentic benchmarks using a sandboxed interpreter increased on computational biology tasks by 36-63 points. Interpretation: Benchmarking is essential to assess the impact and validity of LLMs for medical applications. BenchmarkHub allows a fair and rigorous comparison of models across established datasets, including the possibility to upload their own datasets. The suite includes visual tools to ease model comparison and ranking without any programming knowledge. Self-hosted infrastructure that records every choice and parameter makes benchmark claims checkable without data leaving the institution.

papers.title: Systematic Benchmarking and Optimization of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for Clinical Phenotyping: A Type II Diabetes Case Study in an ICD-Screened Cohort
papers.abstract: Traditional EHR phenotyping methods can require substantial disease-specific development and long-term maintenance. While integrating large language models (LLMs) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is promising, the impact of RAG configurations remains underexplored. We systematically evaluated these design choices for type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) phenotyping in an ICD-screened cohort. Using GPT-4o, we processed 170,678 clinical notes from 275 patients. We evaluated seven embedding models and three prompt strategies (baseline, improved zero-shot, and few-shot). Using the improved zero-shot prompt, we tested 350 embedding model-chunk size-retrieval depth combinations on the training set and selected eight optimized configurations for test-set evaluation. Combined with three prompts, these yielded 24 prompt-configuration combinations for comparison with ICD codes and the institutional PheNorm method. RAG achieved a mean sensitivity of 0.9019 (95% CI: 0.8866-0.9172), specificity of 0.7907 (0.7749-0.8066), PPV of 0.9405 (0.9365-0.9445), NPV of 0.6967 (0.6653-0.7281), and F1-score of 0.9204 (0.9124-0.9283). All combinations achieved higher PPV than ICD codes (0.7838). Compared with PheNorm, sensitivity was significantly higher (Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), while specificity differences were not significant. Paired bootstrap analyses showed higher NPV and F1-score , with no significant PPV difference. General-purpose embeddings showed higher sensitivity, whereas biomedical embeddings exhibited higher specificity and PPV. Few-shot prompting increased specificity and PPV but reduced sensitivity. Token usage varied substantially across embedding models. These findings suggest the importance of aligning RAG design with task-specific clinical priorities and token efficiency.

papers.title: Expert-level localization of fine-grained cardiac structures across the transthoracic echocardiogram
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence models for echocardiography interpret studies without identifying the structures that support their outputs. We show that this spatial grounding does not emerge from the pretraining of current vision-language models. General-purpose and medical vision-language models and an open-vocabulary detector recalled 3% or fewer of cardiac structures and scored below a box that never sees the image. EchoLens, a detector trained on 5,912 expert-annotated structures and 4,219 Doppler signals from 136 patients, recalled 87% and localized structures as reliably as a blinded expert reader (box centre within the reference in 95.7% and 95.3% of cases). It covers 21 structures across 11 transthoracic views and 11 spectral Doppler signal types. In external data, two physicians judged 81-92% of its detections correct across all 11 views, and it identified the Doppler signal type in 83% of frames. EchoLens provides the spatial layer that grounded echocardiographic interpretation requires.

papers.title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa in bronchiectasis: unmasking population diversity and antimicrobial resistance in the Australian context
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections in bronchiectasis airways result in poorer lung function, advanced lung lobe involvement, worsened life quality, and higher hospitalisation rates. Despite high prevalence, little is known about P. aeruginosa population genomics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rates, persistence, and transmission dynamics in Australians with bronchiectasis. Methods: P. aeruginosa (n=137) isolated between 2009 and 2025 from 59 Australians with bronchiectasis underwent antimicrobial susceptibility testing against 11 antipseudomonal drugs, whole-genome sequencing, comparative genomics, and in silico AMR determinant identification. Data were integrated with 4,575 publicly available bronchiectasis-derived P. aeruginosa genomes to determine global phylogenomic and AMR determinant patterns. Results: High AMR rates were identified in the Australian isolates, with 75.9% resistant to at least one antimicrobial, 19.7% multidrug-resistant, and 9.5% extremely drug-resistant. AMR rates were highest (64.2%) for ciprofloxacin and cefepime (44.5%), and lowest for piperacillin/tazobactam (8.8%) and colistin (0.7%). Phylogenomics uncovered several instances of within-host evolution, hypermutation, persistence, and multi-lineage infections. Of the fifty-seven identified multilocus sequence types (STs), seven (12.3%) were novel, five were high-risk international clones (ST274 [6.6%], ST395 [0.7%], ST244 [0.7%], ST277 [0.7%], ST298 [0.7%]) and three were common global clones (ST253 [5.1%], ST155 [3.6%], ST260 [0.7%]). No high-risk AMR-conferring mobile genetic elements were seen, although numerous chromosomal AMR determinants were identified. AMR determinant prevalence was consistent with the global dataset, with no evidence of geographic clustering. Conclusions: Our study provides critical insights into P. aeruginosa diversity in Australians with bronchiectasis. High AMR rates and chronic colonisation highlight the need to improve diagnostics, antimicrobial stewardship measures, and infection control practices in this neglected clinical cohort.

papers.title: In-country cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic next generation sequencing for pathogen detection in Lima, Peru
papers.abstract: Background: Central nervous system (CNS) infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality in low- and middle-income countries such as Peru. However, their epidemiology is poorly characterized due to a wide range of endemic and opportunistic pathogens involved and limited access to specialized neurodiagnostic testing. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) can detect any pathogen in a single hypothesis-free assay but has largely been confined to reference laboratories in high-income countries due to high cost and infrastructure requirements. We piloted an in-country, research-based CSF mNGS protocol in Lima, Peru, as a proof-of-concept study to assess the feasibility of implementing this approach in a resource-limited setting. Methods: Adults admitted with suspected CNS infection at Hospital Nacional Dos de Mayo, a large public hospital in Lima, were enrolled from August 2024 to April 2025, and approximately 0.5-2 mL of surplus CSF was collected. CSF mNGS (DNA and RNA) was performed in-country on a benchtop sequencer with half-volume library reactions and cloud-based analysis (CZID). Paired sequencing at a significantly higher depth was performed on a subset of samples in the United States for validation. Results: Among 43 participants (median age 48 years; 21% living with HIV), mNGS performed in Peru detected 20 pathogens in 18 samples (42%), of which 65% were not identified by routine clinical testing. Nine of 15 patients treated empirically for tuberculous meningitis were found to have a non-mycobacterial infection. Detected organisms included Toxoplasma gondii, Taenia solium, Treponema pallidum, human T-lymphotropic virus 1, herpesviruses, and, on deeper sequencing, Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus. Deep sequencing yielded 3.7-fold (DNA) and 6.9-fold (RNA) more reads and recovered four pathogens missed at shallower-depth. Conclusions: In-country CSF mNGS was feasible in Lima, Peru and recovered a clinically and epidemiologically meaningful spectrum of CNS pathogens, most missed by routine testing. By utilizing available, lower-output sequencers, we overcame a principal barrier to deploying this technology where the burden of undiagnosed CNS infection is greatest.
